relevance_note: A 1984 neuropathological case report of one adult woman (MG) proposed to have Alexander disease ("this may be an adult form of Alexander's disease"); no GFAP gene testing is reported (GFAP appears only as an immunostain), and one previously published case (Patient 3 of Herndon et al) is described with individual-level facts.
method_note: Read and transcribed by hand; no script transcription of tables (the paper has none). No GFAP variant is reported for anyone: 'GFAP' in the paper is the glial fibrillary acid protein stain, so the variants table is empty. MG is in scope through the authors' diagnosis (title; 'this may be an adult form of Alexander's disease'), which they present as a hypothesis based on necropsy; perinatal hypoxia is raised as an alternative cause of her lifelong deficit. Age at onset recorded as the start of the progressive decline at 39 years; the paper also describes delayed motor milestones and mild mental handicap from birth and seizures from age 3, which the authors say may or may not be early manifestations. Patient 3 of Herndon et al (ref 4) is included as a previously published person with individual-level facts (sex, features, death); the present authors doubt her Alexander disease classification. The other three group (b) cases (refs 17, 18, 19) are described only at group level ('all had additional abnormal physical signs such as...') and get no rows; MG's normal male sibling is neither tested nor affected and gets no row. Normal findings recorded as excluded abnormalities (D-27); 'Examination revealed no significant abnormalities outside the nervous system' and 'Routine haematological and biochemical investigations were normal' exclude nothing more specific (the latter recorded as written). Checklist: head circumference 'at the upper limit of normality' excludes macrocephaly only, so 'macrocephaly or megalencephaly' is not reported (brain weight 1600 g given without interpretation); normal eye movements do not address diplopia, so that item is not reported; CSF under normal pressure does not address hydrocephalus, so that item is not reported; cerebral white matter and basal ganglia items are from necropsy histology and CT. Possible tension: CT showed 'slight dilatation' of the ventricles while necropsy 'showed no significant ventricular dilatation'; both recorded as separate rows. Publication year is not printed (only received/accepted dates in 1983), so year is null; n_patients_reported is null because no patient with a GFAP variant is stated.

span: Histologically, our case demonstrated the classical findings of Alexander's disease with diffuse demyelination and extensive Rosenthal fibre formation most marked in perivascular areas.
The staining characteristics confirmed that these were Rosenthal fibres as described in Alexander's disease and other conditions.
The hypothesis that this may be an adult form of Alexander's disease is discussed.
